questions.subject: Botany
questions.stem: In which type of phyllotaxy are two leaves borne at each node on opposite sides of the stem, as seen in Calotropis?
questions.explanation: In opposite phyllotaxy, a pair of leaves arises at each node on opposite sides of the stem. Alternate phyllotaxy has one leaf per node, whorled has three or more, and rosette has leaves clustered at the base.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.topic: Morphology of Flowering Plants: Leaf types
questions.stem: In which type of compound leaf do all the leaflets arise from a common point at the tip of the petiole, as in the silk cotton tree?
questions.explanation: In a palmately compound leaf, the leaflets radiate from one common point at the apex of the petiole. In a pinnately compound leaf, leaflets are arranged along a common axis called the rachis.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.stem: In which type of aestivation do the petals overlap so that one petal is wholly outer, one petal is wholly inner, and the remaining petals overlap on both sides?
questions.explanation: Imbricate aestivation has this arrangement of one outermost petal, one innermost petal, and the remaining petals overlapping on both sides. Valvate petals just touch at their margins without overlapping, and twisted petals overlap in one direction only.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.stem: Which type of covalent bond links adjacent nucleotides together in a polynucleotide chain?
questions.explanation: Adjacent nucleotides are joined by a phosphodiester linkage between the 3′-OH of one pentose sugar and the phosphate attached to the 5′-carbon of the next. Glycosidic bonds join sugars, peptide bonds join amino acids, and hydrogen bonds stabilise base pairing rather than linking nucleotides covalently.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.stem: Which polysaccharide serves as the principal storage carbohydrate in animal cells?
questions.explanation: Glycogen is the animal storage polysaccharide, stored mainly in liver and skeletal muscle. Starch is the plant storage form, cellulose is a structural component of plant cell walls, and inulin is a fructose polymer stored in some plants.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.stem: An enzyme-catalysed reaction is run in the presence of a fixed concentration of a competitive inhibitor. When the substrate concentration is increased far above the Michaelis constant (Km), what happens to the reaction velocity?
options: It approaches the same maximum velocity (Vmax) as the uninhibited reaction
It rises above the uninhibited Vmax
It remains permanently at half of the uninhibited Vmax
It falls to zero because the enzyme is irreversibly blocked
questions.explanation: A competitive inhibitor competes with the substrate for the active site, so at very high substrate concentration the substrate outcompetes it and Vmax is reached. Competitive inhibition raises the apparent Km but does not change Vmax.

questions.subject: Zoology

B. Saturated fatty acids always contain at least one carbon-carbon double bond.
C. Phospholipids have both a hydrophilic head and hydrophobic fatty acid tails.
Select the correct option.
questions.explanation: Triglycerides are glycerol esterified with three fatty acids, and phospholipids are amphipathic with a polar head and non-polar tails. Saturated fatty acids have no double bonds, so statement B is false.

A is true but R is false.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.stem: Which type of synovial joint allows rotation of the head around the axis formed by the atlas and axis vertebrae?
questions.explanation: The atlas rotates on the axis (dens) at the pivot joint, which permits rotation of the head. Ball and socket joints allow movement in multiple planes, hinge joints permit flexion and extension only, and gliding joints allow sliding between flat bone surfaces.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.stem: How many bones are present in the appendicular skeleton of an adult human?
questions.explanation: The adult human skeleton has 206 bones, of which 80 form the axial skeleton and 126 form the appendicular skeleton. The number 22 corresponds to the bones of the skull, which belong to the axial skeleton.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.stem: During skeletal muscle contraction, which protein complex binds Ca²⁺ and, after binding, shifts tropomyosin away from the myosin-binding sites on actin?
questions.explanation: Troponin is the complex on the thin filament that binds Ca²⁺ released into the sarcoplasm. This binding moves tropomyosin off the active sites on actin, allowing cross-bridge formation with myosin.

questions.subject: Zoology

Consider the following statements about locomotion and movement:

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.topic: Disorders of the muscular and skeletal systems

C. Osteoporosis | III. Autoimmune attack on acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction
D. Gout | IV. Decrease in bone mass and density
Choose the correct option.
questions.explanation: Myasthenia gravis results from autoimmune attack on acetylcholine receptors (III), and muscular dystrophy from defective dystrophin (II). Osteoporosis involves loss of bone mass and density (IV), while gout is caused by uric acid crystal deposition in joints (I).

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.stem: Dark-coloured (melanic) moths became more common than light-coloured moths in industrial areas of England after soot covered tree trunks. Which process best explains this change in the population?
options: Natural selection favouring camouflage in a changed environment
Genetic drift in a small isolated population
questions.explanation: Dark moths survived better on soot-darkened bark and left more offspring, so the environment selected for their variant. This is natural selection, as described in NCERT's industrial melanism example.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.stem: Which of the following best illustrates adaptive radiation?
options: Several species of finches on the Galápagos Islands, each with a different beak shape suited to its food
Wings of bats and wings of birds having a common basic bone plan
Eyes of the octopus and eyes of mammals developing independently
Flippers of whales and forelimbs of horses
questions.explanation: Adaptive radiation is the evolution of many species from a single ancestor in different directions, each adapted to a different niche. Darwin's finches on the Galápagos Islands are the classic example.

questions.subject: Zoology

A. Heritable variations arise randomly and natural selection acts on them.
B. Organs that are used more become larger in the next generation because acquired characters are inherited.
C. Mutation is the ultimate source of new variation in a population.
Choose the correct option.
questions.explanation: Statement A and C are correct, as variations arise randomly and mutations are the ultimate source of variation. Statement B describes Lamarck's inheritance of acquired characters, which is not accepted as an explanation of evolution.

Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Zoology

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.stem: In a myelinated nerve fibre, the nerve impulse appears to jump from one node of Ranvier to the next. This mode of impulse conduction is called:
questions.explanation: Depolarisation occurs only at the nodes of Ranvier because the myelin sheath insulates the internodal regions, so the impulse jumps between nodes. This is called saltatory conduction.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.stem: During the rising phase of an action potential, the membrane potential of a neuron changes from about -70 mV to about +30 mV. Which ion movement is mainly responsible for this change?

Influx of Na⁺ into the axon
Influx of Cl⁻ into the axon
Efflux of Na⁺ from the axon
questions.explanation: The rising phase is caused by a rapid increase in membrane permeability to Na⁺, which flows into the axon down its electrochemical gradient. Efflux of K⁺ is responsible for repolarisation instead.

questions.topic: Neural control: parts of the brain

Anode, because DNA is positively charged
Anode, because DNA is negatively charged due to phosphate groups

questions.subject: Zoology

The presence of a stop codon in the Cry gene of the plant
The temperature at which the plant tissue is grown
The presence of specific receptor proteins on the midgut epithelial cells of the insect

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.stem: Which cells form the myelin sheath around axons in the brain and spinal cord?
questions.explanation: In the central nervous system, myelin sheaths are produced by oligodendrocytes, whereas Schwann cells perform this role in the peripheral nervous system. Astrocytes and microglia do not form myelin.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.stem: In a myelinated nerve fibre, the nerve impulse jumps from one node of Ranvier to the next. This mode of impulse conduction is called:
questions.explanation: Myelin acts as an insulator, so depolarisation occurs only at the nodes of Ranvier and the impulse appears to jump between them. This is called saltatory conduction, which is faster than continuous conduction in unmyelinated fibres.
questions.source_name: AI-written practice question; answer independently checked by a second AI model. Not expert-reviewed.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.topic: Neural control: brain regions and their functions
questions.stem:
Read the following statements about the human brain.
A. The cerebrum is the seat of voluntary actions, memory and intelligence.
B. The medulla oblongata controls involuntary activities such as respiration and heartbeat.
C. The hypothalamus contains centres that regulate body temperature and hunger.
D. The corpus callosum is a part of the hindbrain and controls posture and balance.
Which of the above statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Statements A, B and C correctly describe the functions of the cerebrum, medulla oblongata and hypothalamus. Statement D is wrong because the corpus callosum is a band of nerve fibres in the forebrain (cerebrum), not the hindbrain, and posture is controlled by the cerebellum.
questions.source_name: AI-written practice question; answer independently checked by a second AI model. Not expert-reviewed.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.stem: During the rising phase of an action potential in a nerve axon, which ionic movement across the axonal membrane is mainly responsible for the depolarisation?
questions.explanation: At the stimulus threshold, voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open and Na⁺ rushes into the axon, making the inside of the membrane positive. This sodium influx produces the rising phase of the action potential.
questions.source_name: AI-written practice question; answer independently checked by a second AI model. Not expert-reviewed.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.stem:
Read the assertion and reason and choose the correct option.
Assertion (A): Transmission across a chemical synapse is unidirectional.
Reason (R): Neurotransmitters are released only from the presynaptic knob and bind only to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
questions.explanation: Both statements are true, and the one-way flow of the impulse across a chemical synapse follows from neurotransmitter release only from the presynaptic terminal and binding only to postsynaptic receptors. The reason correctly explains the assertion.

questions.topic: Neural control: structure and function of the eye
questions.stem:

B. Cone cells | II. Vision in dim light
C. Fovea | III. Region of maximum visual acuity
D. Blind spot | IV. Colour vision in bright light

questions.explanation: Rods function in dim light (A-II), cones give colour vision in bright light (B-IV), the fovea has the highest visual acuity (C-III), and the blind spot has no photoreceptors (D-I).

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.stem: Which component of human blood is primarily responsible for transporting oxygen from the lungs to the body tissues?
questions.explanation: Erythrocytes (red blood cells) contain haemoglobin, which binds oxygen in the lungs and releases it in tissues. Leucocytes defend the body, thrombocytes help in clotting, and plasma mainly transports dissolved substances.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about lymph:
A. Lymph lacks erythrocytes.
B. Lymph contains lymphocytes that take part in immune responses.
C. Lymph has a higher concentration of plasma proteins than blood plasma.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: Lymph is a colourless fluid without RBCs but with lymphocytes, so A and B are correct. Lymph has fewer plasma proteins than blood plasma because large proteins are largely retained in the blood, so C is false.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.stem: In a standard ECG, which wave or complex represents the depolarisation of the ventricles?
questions.explanation: The P wave represents atrial depolarisation, while the QRS complex represents ventricular depolarisation that precedes ventricular contraction. The T wave represents ventricular repolarisation.
questions.source_name: AI-written practice question; answer independently checked by a second AI model. Not expert-reviewed.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.stem:
Match List-I with List-II.
A. Tricuspid valve | I. Guards the opening between left atrium and left ventricle
B. Bicuspid valve | II. Guards the opening between right atrium and right ventricle
C. Semilunar valves | III. Prevent backflow of blood from aorta and pulmonary artery into ventricles
D. Chordae tendineae | IV. Prevent valves from being pushed back into the atria during ventricular contraction
questions.explanation: The tricuspid valve lies between the right atrium and right ventricle, and the bicuspid (mitral) valve lies between the left atrium and left ventricle. Semilunar valves prevent backflow into the ventricles, and chordae tendineae stop the atrioventricular valves from inverting into the atria.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.stem: Which plasma protein is converted into fibrin during the clotting of blood?
questions.explanation: Fibrinogen, a soluble plasma protein, is converted into insoluble fibrin threads by the enzyme thrombin during clot formation. Albumin and globulins do not form the clot network, and haemoglobin is an intracellular protein of erythrocytes.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.stem: Which hormone, secreted by the adrenal medulla during stress, increases heart rate and blood glucose level?
questions.explanation: Adrenaline (epinephrine) is secreted by the adrenal medulla in emergency or stress conditions. It increases heart beat, raises blood pressure and mobilises glucose from glycogen.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.stem: Which of the following hormones exerts its effect by binding to an intracellular receptor and regulating gene expression?
questions.explanation: Thyroid hormones are iodinated amino acid derivatives that are lipophilic enough to cross the plasma membrane and bind intracellular receptors, which then regulate transcription. Adrenaline, glucagon and insulin are peptide or amine hormones that act through membrane receptors and second messengers.
questions.source_name: AI-written practice question; answer independently checked by a second AI model. Not expert-reviewed.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about hormones and blood calcium.
A. Parathyroid hormone increases blood calcium levels.
B. Calcitonin is secreted by the parathyroid glands.
C. Deficiency of thyroid hormone in adults can lead to myxoedema.
D. Glucagon lowers blood glucose levels.
Which statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Parathyroid hormone raises blood calcium, and hypothyroidism in adults causes myxoedema. Calcitonin is secreted by the thyroid (not parathyroid), and glucagon raises blood glucose, so only A and C are correct.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.stem:

B. Cretinism | II. Hypersecretion of growth hormone in adults
C. Diabetes mellitus | III. Hyposecretion of thyroid in childhood
D. Tetany | IV. Hyperglycaemia due to insulin deficiency
Choose the correct option.
questions.explanation: Acromegaly results from excess growth hormone in adults, cretinism from thyroid hyposecretion in childhood, diabetes mellitus from insulin deficiency with hyperglycaemia, and tetany from low blood calcium. This gives A-II, B-III, C-IV, D-I.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.stem: A tumour develops in the zona reticularis of the adrenal cortex. Which category of hormones is most likely to be secreted in excess?
questions.explanation: The zona reticularis of the adrenal cortex secretes sex corticoids, mainly androgens. Aldosterone comes from the zona glomerulosa, cortisol mainly from the zona fasciculata, and adrenaline is from the adrenal medulla.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.stem: Which enzyme is used to join the sugar-phosphate backbones of a cut vector and a foreign DNA fragment during recombinant DNA construction?
questions.explanation: DNA ligase seals nicks by forming phosphodiester bonds between the 3′-OH and 5′-phosphate ends of DNA fragments. Restriction endonucleases cut DNA, so they do not join it.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.stem: What property of restriction endonucleases makes them useful as molecular scissors for cloning?
options: They recognise random nucleotide sequences in DNA
They cut only single-stranded RNA molecules
They are active only in the absence of Mg²⁺ ions
They recognise palindromic nucleotide sequences and cut DNA at those sites
questions.explanation: Restriction enzymes recognise specific palindromic sequences and cleave DNA within or near them, producing defined fragments. Their activity depends on Mg²⁺, so the last option is false.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.stem: During agarose gel electrophoresis, DNA fragments migrate towards which electrode, and why?
options: Anode, because DNA is positively charged
Anode, because DNA is negatively charged
Cathode, because DNA is positively charged
Cathode, because DNA is negatively charged
questions.explanation: The sugar-phosphate backbone of DNA carries a net negative charge, so DNA moves towards the positive electrode, the anode. Smaller fragments move faster through the agarose matrix.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about cloning vectors and related tools.
A. The ori is the sequence from which replication of the vector starts in the host cell.
B. A selectable marker, such as an antibiotic resistance gene, helps in identifying transformants.
C. Agrobacterium tumefaciens is used to introduce DNA directly into bacterial cells without any plasmid.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: Statements A and B correctly describe the ori and selectable marker in a vector. Statement C is wrong because Agrobacterium transfers DNA through its Ti plasmid in plants, not directly into bacteria.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.stem:
Assertion (A): On X-gal medium, colonies carrying a recombinant plasmid with an insert in the lacZ gene appear white.
Reason (R): Insertion of foreign DNA into lacZ disrupts β-galactosidase production, so X-gal is not converted to a blue product.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
questions.explanation: Insertional inactivation of lacZ stops β-galactosidase formation, so the chromogenic substrate is not hydrolysed and colonies stay white. The reason correctly explains the assertion.

questions.stem:
Match List-I with List-II
A. Restriction endonuclease | I. Joins DNA fragments by forming phosphodiester bonds
B. Exonuclease | II. Cuts DNA at specific palindromic sites
C. DNA ligase | III. Removes nucleotides from the ends of a DNA strand
D. DNA polymerase | IV. Synthesises a new DNA strand using a template
questions.explanation: Restriction endonucleases cut at palindromic sites (A-II), exonucleases remove terminal nucleotides (B-III), ligases join fragments (C-I), and DNA polymerase synthesises DNA on a template (D-IV).

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.topic: Evidence for evolution: homology and analogy
questions.stem: The wings of a butterfly and the wings of a pigeon perform the same function of flight, but they have different basic structural plans and embryonic origins. What are such structures called?
questions.explanation: Structures with the same function but different fundamental design and origin are analogous organs, which show convergent evolution. Homologous organs share a basic structural plan inherited from a common ancestor, despite differing in function.
questions.source_name: AI-written practice question; answer independently checked by a second AI model. Not expert-reviewed.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.stem: In a population of birds, individuals with medium-sized body weight survive best, while those with very small or very large body weight are eliminated. Which mode of natural selection is operating?
questions.explanation: Stabilising selection favours the average or intermediate phenotype and eliminates extremes at both ends of the range. Directional selection would shift the population mean toward one extreme, and disruptive selection would favour both extremes.
questions.source_name: AI-written practice question; answer independently checked by a second AI model. Not expert-reviewed.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.stem: A small group of individuals breaks away from a large parent population and settles in a new, isolated area. The allele frequencies in the new colony differ noticeably from those of the parent population because the founders carried only a sample of the parental gene pool. Which process best explains this change?
questions.explanation: The founder effect is a form of genetic drift in which a new population established by a few individuals has a non-representative subset of the parental alleles. Gene flow would instead tend to make populations more similar, and mutation alone is not the explanation described.
questions.source_name: AI-written practice question; answer independently checked by a second AI model. Not expert-reviewed.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.stem:
Which of the following statements about the origin of life are correct?
A. Miller's experiment used CH₄, H₂, NH₃ and water vapour in a closed apparatus.
B. Oparin and Haldane proposed that the early atmosphere was reducing in nature.
C. Miller's experiment produced nucleic acids from the simulated atmosphere.
questions.explanation: Miller's apparatus contained CH₄, H₂, NH₃ and water vapour, and Oparin and Haldane proposed a reducing early atmosphere, so A and B are correct. Miller's experiment produced amino acids and other organic molecules, not nucleic acids, so C is incorrect.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.stem:
Assertion (A): In some male birds, elaborate tail feathers can reduce their chances of escaping predators.
Reason (R): Traits that increase success in obtaining mates can be retained by natural selection even when they lower individual survival.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
questions.explanation: Elaborate ornaments can be a survival disadvantage, and sexual selection can maintain them because they improve mating success, so both statements are true and R explains A. Fitness is measured by reproductive success, which is why such traits persist.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.topic: Evidences of evolution: vestigial organs, analogy, atavism, fossils

B. Analogous organs | II. Archaeopteryx
C. Atavism | III. Human appendix
D. Connecting link fossil | IV. Human baby born with a tail
questions.explanation: The human appendix is a vestigial organ, and butterfly and bird wings are analogous organs. A tail in a human baby is an example of atavism, and Archaeopteryx is a connecting link fossil showing reptile and bird features.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.topic: Hormonal regulation of the menstrual cycle
questions.stem: Which hormone, secreted by the corpus luteum, is essential for maintaining the endometrium during the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle?
questions.explanation: After ovulation the corpus luteum secretes progesterone, which maintains the thickened endometrium needed for implantation. FSH and LH act mainly on the ovary and pituitary feedback, and prolactin is not a corpus luteum hormone.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.stem: Which contraceptive method provides a physical barrier that prevents sperms from entering the female reproductive tract, and is also useful in preventing sexually transmitted infections?
questions.explanation: A male condom is a barrier method that stops sperms from reaching the female genital tract and also reduces the risk of STIs. Pills act hormonally, while tubectomy and vasectomy are surgical methods.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.stem: In which assisted reproductive technique is a zygote or early embryo with up to eight blastomeres transferred into the fallopian tube of the female?
questions.explanation: In ZIFT, fertilisation occurs outside the body and the zygote or early embryo is placed in the fallopian tube. In GIFT, gametes rather than a zygote are transferred, while IUT places the embryo directly into the uterus.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about the menstrual cycle in a human female.
A. The menstrual phase typically lasts 3 to 5 days and is caused by a fall in progesterone and oestrogen levels.
B. Ovulation occurs around the middle of a 28-day cycle and is triggered by a surge in LH.
C. The proliferative phase is marked by a fall in circulating oestrogen.
questions.explanation: Statements A and B match the NCERT description of menstruation and the LH-triggered ovulation around day 14. Statement C is wrong because the proliferative phase is characterised by rising oestrogen, which rebuilds the endometrium.

Assertion (A): Vasectomy is a surgical method of male contraception that does not interfere with the production of male sex hormones.

Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
questions.explanation: Both statements are true, and blocking the vas deferens explains why sperms are prevented from being ejaculated, while hormone production by the testes continues unaffected. The reason correctly explains the assertion.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.stem: Which bacterium is the causative agent of typhoid fever in humans, spread through contaminated food and water?
questions.explanation: Typhoid fever is caused by Salmonella typhi, which enters the body through contaminated food and water and infects the intestine and blood. The other three bacteria cause cholera, dysentery and tetanus respectively.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.stem: A person bitten by a snake is given a preformed antiserum containing antibodies against the snake venom. Which type of immunity does the person acquire?
questions.explanation: Antibodies readymade in another organism and injected into the patient provide passive immunity, which acts immediately but is short-lived. Active immunity develops when the body itself produces antibodies in response to an antigen.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.stem: In a human patient with Plasmodium vivax malaria, the periodic chill and high fever coincide with which event in the erythrocytic cycle?
options: Entry of sporozoites into liver cells
Rupture of infected RBCs releasing merozoites
Formation of gametocytes in the blood
Penetration of the mosquito midgut by ookinetes
questions.explanation: Fever in malaria is synchronised with the rupture of infected red blood cells, which releases merozoites and toxic substances into the blood. Sporozoite entry into liver cells occurs before the blood stage, and gametocytes and ookinetes do not cause the periodic fever.

Consider the following statements about cancer:
A. Proto-oncogenes are normal cellular genes that can be converted into oncogenes under certain conditions.
B. Cancer cells lose contact inhibition and divide in an uncontrolled manner.
C. Benign tumours readily invade surrounding tissues and spread to distant organs by metastasis.
D. Certain chemicals and radiations can act as carcinogens that cause cancer.

questions.explanation: Statements A, B and D agree with NCERT: proto-oncogenes can become oncogenes, cancer cells lose contact inhibition, and carcinogens include chemicals and radiation. Statement C is wrong because benign tumours do not metastasise, while malignant tumours do.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.stem: How many peptide bonds are present in a linear tetrapeptide?
questions.explanation: A linear peptide with n amino acids has n−1 peptide bonds. A tetrapeptide has four amino acids, so it has three peptide bonds.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.stem: In a double-stranded DNA molecule, adenine makes up 28% of the total bases. What percentage of the bases is cytosine?
questions.explanation: Chargaff's rules state that A equals T and G equals C. Since A is 28%, the remaining 44% is split equally between G and C, so cytosine is 22%.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.topic: Amino acids: zwitterions and isoelectric point
questions.stem: At its isoelectric point, glycine exists predominantly as which of the following species?
options: A neutral molecule with no ionisable groups
A zwitterion with net charge zero
questions.explanation: At the isoelectric point, the amino acid carries both a protonated amino group (NH₃⁺) and a deprotonated carboxylate group (COO⁻), so it is a zwitterion with zero net charge. It is not a neutral molecule without ionisable groups.

questions.topic: Nucleic acids: structure of DNA and RNA

A. The sugar in DNA is deoxyribose.
B. Adenine pairs with thymine in DNA through two hydrogen bonds.
C. RNA is usually a double-stranded molecule.
D. Cytosine and thymine are purine bases.

questions.explanation: Statements A and B are correct, since DNA contains deoxyribose and the A–T pair is joined by two hydrogen bonds. RNA is usually single-stranded, and cytosine and thymine are pyrimidines, not purines.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.stem: Which segment of the nephron is impermeable to water but actively pumps out Na⁺ and Cl⁻, thereby contributing to the hyperosmotic medullary interstitium?
options: Ascending limb of loop of Henle
Descending limb of loop of Henle
questions.explanation: The thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle is impermeable to water, and its active transport of salts into the medullary interstitium builds the osmotic gradient essential for concentrating urine. The descending limb is permeable to water and loses water instead.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.topic: Nitrogenous wastes and types of excretion
questions.stem: In ureotelic animals such as adult humans, urea is synthesised through a cycle that operates mainly in which organ?
questions.explanation: Urea is formed through the ornithine cycle, which operates in the liver of ureotelic animals. The kidney only excretes the urea and does not synthesise it, while gills are associated with ammonia loss in aquatic animals.

A. Juxtamedullary nephrons have long loops of Henle that extend deep into the medulla.
B. Vasa recta runs alongside the loops of Henle and helps maintain the medullary osmotic gradient.
C. Renin is secreted by the macula densa cells of the distal convoluted tubule.
D. Podocytes are present in the wall of the descending limb of loop of Henle.
Which statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Juxtamedullary nephrons have long loops that dip into the medulla, and vasa recta supports the medullary gradient, so A and B are correct. Renin is released by juxtaglomerular cells of the afferent arteriole, and podocytes line the Bowman's capsule, so C and D are wrong.

Glucose and amino acid reabsorption occurs mainly in the proximal convoluted tubule (C-IV), while H⁺ and K⁺ secretion occurs in the distal convoluted tubule (D-I).

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.topic: Evidences of evolution: homologous and analogous organs

options: Pentadactyl limbs of lizard and frog
Wings of butterfly and wings of bird
Wings of bat and forelimbs of cat
questions.explanation: Butterfly and bird wings perform the same function but have different basic structural plans and arose independently, so they are analogous. The other pairs share a common fundamental plan inherited from a common ancestor, so they are homologous.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.stem: In a large population in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, the frequency of allele A is 0.7 and of allele a is 0.3. What is the frequency of heterozygotes (Aa)?
questions.explanation: Heterozygote frequency equals 2pq, which is 2 × 0.7 × 0.3 = 0.42. The value 0.49 is p², the frequency of AA homozygotes, and 0.09 is q².

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.topic: Factors affecting gene pool: genetic drift
questions.stem: The founder effect is best described as
options: Random change in allele frequency when a small group of individuals separates from a larger population and establishes a new population
Non-random mating that increases homozygosity in a large population
Increase in mutation rate caused by exposure to radiation
Migration of individuals that makes two populations genetically identical
questions.explanation: The founder effect is a type of genetic drift in which a small founding group carries only a sample of the parent population's alleles, so the new population's allele frequencies differ by chance. The other options describe different processes.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about the origin of life.
A. Miller's experiment simulated early Earth conditions using methane, ammonia, hydrogen and water vapour and produced amino acids.
B. The experiment supported the idea that simple organic molecules can form abiotically under primitive atmospheric conditions.
C. Oparin and Haldane proposed that the early atmosphere of Earth was highly oxidising.
D. In Miller's setup, living cells arose directly from non-living chemicals.
Which statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Miller's experiment produced amino acids under a reducing atmosphere, supporting chemical evolution, so A and B are correct. Oparin and Haldane proposed a reducing (not oxidising) early atmosphere, and Miller did not produce living cells, so C and D are wrong.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.topic: Mechanism of evolution: natural selection and gene pool
questions.stem:
Assertion (A): Natural selection acts directly on phenotypes, yet evolution is measured as a change in allele frequencies in a population's gene pool.
Reason (R): Phenotypic variations acquired by an organism during its lifetime due to environmental influence are passed on to its offspring.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
questions.explanation: Natural selection acts on phenotypes, but the heritable units that change over generations are alleles in the gene pool, so A is true. Traits acquired during lifetime due to environment are not genetically inherited, so R is false.

B. Analogous organs | II. Divergent evolution
C. Connecting link | III. Intermediate form showing features of two groups
D. Vestigial organ | IV. Non-functional reduced structure
Choose the correct match.
questions.explanation: Homologous organs arise through divergent evolution (A-II), and analogous organs arise through convergent evolution (B-I). Connecting links show features of two groups (C-III), and vestigial organs are reduced non-functional structures (D-IV).

Glycosidic bonds between adjacent amino acid residues
Ionic bonds between charged side chains of distant residues
Hydrogen bonds between the C=O of one amino acid residue and the N-H of a residue four positions ahead
questions.explanation: In the α-helix, hydrogen bonds form between the carbonyl oxygen of one residue and the amide hydrogen of the residue four positions ahead, holding the helical coil together. Disulphide bridges and ionic bonds contribute to tertiary structure, and glycosidic bonds link sugars, not amino acids.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explanation: A-T pairs form two hydrogen bonds and G-C pairs form three, so A and B are correct. The two strands of DNA are antiparallel (run in opposite directions), so C is incorrect.

A is true but R is false.

questions.explanation: Denaturation disrupts hydrogen bonds and other weak interactions, which destroys higher-order structure, while the covalent peptide bonds of the primary structure remain intact. The reason is true and correctly explains why the primary structure survives.

questions.subject: Zoology

questions.explanation: Three distinct amino acids can be arranged in 3! = 3 × 2 × 1 = 6 different orders, and each order gives a different tripeptide sequence.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.stem: Which somatic cells of the seminiferous tubules provide nutrition to the developing sperms and are under the control of FSH?
questions.explanation: Sertoli cells nourish the developing germ cells during spermatogenesis and respond to FSH. Leydig cells are interstitial cells that secrete androgens, not nutritive cells for sperms.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.stem: During menstruation, which layer of the uterine wall is shed along with blood vessels?
questions.explanation: The functional layer of the endometrium breaks down and is shed during menstruation when fertilisation has not occurred. The myometrium is the muscular layer and is not shed.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.stem: In a menstrual cycle in which fertilisation does not occur, what follows immediately after the sharp fall in progesterone caused by the degeneration of the corpus luteum?
options: Formation of the placenta from trophoblast cells
Release of a secondary oocyte from the ovary
Thickening of the endometrium due to rising oestrogen
Shedding of the functional layer of the endometrium
questions.explanation: Progesterone maintains the endometrium, so its sharp fall leads to breakdown of the functional layer and menstrual flow. The other options describe events that occur before ovulation or during pregnancy, not after luteal regression.

Consider the following statements about the human placenta.
A. The placenta secretes human chorionic gonadotropin, which sustains the corpus luteum in early pregnancy.
B. The placenta acts as an endocrine tissue that secretes large amounts of oestrogen and progesterone during pregnancy.
C. The placenta is formed exclusively from maternal endometrial tissue, so embryonic and maternal blood mix freely within it.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: Statements A and B are correct, as hCG maintains the corpus luteum and the placenta produces oestrogen and progesterone. Statement C is wrong because the placenta has both embryonic and maternal parts, and the two bloods do not mix.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.

questions.explanation: Oxytocin contracts myoepithelial cells around the alveoli and ducts, which pushes milk toward the nipple. This mechanism explains the milk ejection reflex, so R correctly explains A.

questions.topic: Resting membrane potential and the sodium-potassium pump
questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes the sodium-potassium pump of a resting neuron?
options: It opens voltage-gated Na⁺ channels during depolarisation
It moves Ca²⁺ into the axon to maintain the resting state
It moves 2 Na⁺ out and 3 K⁺ in for every ATP hydrolysed
It moves 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in for every ATP hydrolysed
questions.explanation: The sodium-potassium pump uses ATP to actively transport 3 Na⁺ out of the axon and 2 K⁺ into it. This maintains the concentration gradients that help establish the resting potential.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.stem: A drug blocks voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels in the membrane of the synaptic knob of a chemical synapse. Which event would be most directly prevented?

Opening of Na⁺ channels in the postsynaptic membrane
Release of neurotransmitter into the synaptic cleft
Binding of neurotransmitter to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane
questions.explanation: Arrival of an action potential at the synaptic knob opens voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels, and the Ca²⁺ influx triggers fusion of synaptic vesicles and release of neurotransmitter. Blocking these channels stops this release, while the axonal action potential and the postsynaptic events depend on the released transmitter.

questions.explanation: The cerebellum coordinates voluntary movements and maintains posture and balance. The hypothalamus regulates homeostatic functions, and the medulla oblongata controls vital involuntary activities such as breathing and heart rate.

The protoxin is activated in the acidic stomach of mammals, so it is toxic to them
The toxin is produced only in the root cells and never reaches the leaves
The toxin is a spore coat protein that germinates only in soil
questions.explanation: Cry proteins from Bacillus thuringiensis are protoxins that are solubilised and converted to active toxins in the alkaline midgut of susceptible insects. Human stomach conditions and the absence of suitable receptors make the toxin harmless to humans.

It is obtained from Agrobacterium tumefaciens
It cuts DNA only at palindromic sequences
questions.explanation: PCR involves repeated heat denaturation at around 95°C, which would destroy E. coli DNA polymerase I in every cycle. Taq polymerase is thermostable, so it can be added once and used through many cycles.
